what_its_for: Estrogen is a hormone medicine used to relieve symptoms of menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, and itching. It may also be used to prevent bone loss (osteoporosis) after menopause, treat certain hormone-related conditions, or replace estrogen in women whose ovaries have been removed.
how_to_take: Estrogen comes in several forms — pills, skin patches, gels, creams, vaginal rings, and vaginal tablets. Take pills by mouth with or without food, at the same time each day. Apply patches to clean, dry skin on your belly, buttocks, or upper arm — never on your breasts. Rotate patch sites each time. For gels and creams, apply to the skin exactly as directed by your doctor. For vaginal forms, use the applicator provided and follow the instructions carefully. Wash your hands before and after applying any topical form.
dosing: Your doctor will prescribe the lowest dose that works for you, for the shortest time needed. Dosing varies depending on the form and reason for use. Do not change your dose on your own. Always follow your doctor's instructions. If you are not sure how much to take or apply, call your doctor or pharmacist.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose of your pill, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you forget to change your patch on schedule, apply a new one as soon as you remember and then return to your regular patch-change schedule.
storage: Store pills and patches at room temperature, away from heat, light, and moisture. Do not store them in the bathroom. Keep gels and creams tightly closed. Keep all estrogen products out of reach of children and pets. Used patches still contain active hormone — fold them in half and dispose of them safely in the trash, away from children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid smoking while using estrogen — it greatly increases the risk of serious side effects like blood clots, stroke, and heart attack, especially if you are over 35. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, as it may affect how your body processes estrogen. Do not apply topical estrogen (gels, creams) to your breasts. Avoid letting others — especially children or men — come into contact with areas where you applied estrogen gel or cream, as it can be absorbed through their skin.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have: chest pain or tightness, shortness of breath, sudden severe headache, vision changes, sudden leg pain or swelling, numbness or weakness on one side of your body, or unusual vaginal bleeding. Also call your doctor if you notice a lump in your breast, yellowing of your skin or eyes, severe stomach pain, skin rash or irritation at the patch site that does not go away, or any new or unusual symptoms.
when_it_works: Many women notice improvement in hot flashes and night sweats within a few weeks of starting estrogen. Vaginal symptoms like dryness and discomfort may take a few weeks to a couple of months to improve. Bone-protective effects take longer to become noticeable. Keep taking your medicine even if you feel well — do not stop without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Estrogen should NOT be used during pregnancy or while breastfeeding. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Older adults: Older women (especially over age 65) may have a higher risk of serious side effects including dementia, stroke, and blood clots — your doctor will carefully weigh the risks and benefits. Women with a uterus: If you still have a uterus, your doctor will likely prescribe a progestin along with estrogen to protect the lining of your uterus and reduce the risk of uterine cancer. Women with certain health conditions: Estrogen may not be right for you if you have a history of breast cancer, blood clots, stroke, heart attack, liver disease, or unexplained vaginal bleeding. Always give your doctor your full medical history.
